entries.title: Jeremiah 14:1
segments:
vv 1-6. 
 
God has all the powers of nature under his control.  When he chooses through them to punish nations for their sins, they can neither resist nor endure his hand.

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:2
segments: They are black unto the ground; they lie upon the ground in a squalid and mourning condition.

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:6
segments: They snuffed up the wind; in their endeavors to find water, the direction of which these animals ascertain by the scent.

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:7
segments:
vv 7-9. 
 
In the deepest distress God is able to hear and deliver us; and though on the ground of our own righteousness we can expect nothing but destruction, we may for his name's sake hope that he will save us, when we heartily repent of our iniquities.

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:8
segments: A stranger--a wayfaring man; who only passes through a country without concerning himself with its interests.

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:9
segments: A man astonished--a mighty man; who has heretofore wrought wonders, but whose wisdom and strength now fail him.

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:10
segments:
vv 10-11. 
 
Both nations and individuals may go to such lengths in rebellion and iniquity, that God will hear no intercessory prayer in their behalf.

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:13
segments:
vv 13-16. 
 
Men's readiness, everywhere and in all ages, to listen to those who flatter them and promise them peace and prosperity in sin, is a sad proof of the desperate deceitfulness and wickedness of the human heart.

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:17
segments:
vv 17-19. 
 
The prevalence of national iniquity fills the good man's soul with the deepest grief, both for the glory of God's name, and for the certain ruin, temporal and spiritual, which such iniquity occasions.

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:21
segments: Do not disgrace the throne of thy glory; by giving occasion to thine enemies to blaspheme thy name as unable to save thy people. Compare

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:22
segments:
Can the heavens give showers? that is, of their own proper power. They are God's workmanship, and he alone can control their action. 
 
  All these things; heaven and earth. 
 
In the last four verses of this chapter the prophet speaks in the name of the pious remnant.  From this it is plain that God's command, "Pray not for this people for their good,"

, was not absolute, but a declaration that, while the mass of the people continued impenitent, no prayer could avert his judgments. 
 
To sin against the Author of nature, and then look to the powers of nature for help and deliverance, is the extreme of madness and folly.
